title: The King's Letters of Seoul
logline: From King Sejong's new letters in 1446 to the light of 1945, the detective is a guest at twelve turning points of Korea's story. At each one a short note in the King's letters, marked with a small water drop, asks for help. Who keeps writing them, across five hundred years?

coreMystery.question: Who leaves the notes in the King's letters, marked with a small water drop, at every turning point of Korea's story, and what do they keep?
coreMystery.truth: Bun-i, the water-carrier who wrote the first letter in the new letters in 1446 (Case 01), was given a small wooden letter box by Sora. She taught her children to read, and they taught theirs. For five hundred years one ordinary family, never famous, kept the box: in every hard time a keeper wrote one short note in the King's letters, signed it with Bun-i's water drop, and quietly helped. They never changed history; they kept the letters alive and helped people see the truth.
coreMystery.culprit: No one: the season's mystery is a family of keepers, not a crime. Each case has its own small, made-up wrongdoer or puzzle; history itself is never changed.
coreMystery.motive: To keep the people's own letters alive, as Bun-i promised Sora: 'Anyone can learn them. I will teach them.'
coreMystery.method: A short note in Hangeul with a water-drop mark, left where the detective will find it, in each case; the letter box passed from parent to child.

themes: Letters are for everyone: King Sejong made them so ordinary people could write what they meant.
Ordinary people keep a country's memory: the keepers are never famous.
Evidence over guesses: every case is solved by reading closely.
History is not changed: the detective finds the truth of each moment and sees what really happened.
startingSituation: Autumn 1446: the detective is King Sejong's guest when a half-burnt paper in the new letters is found at the inner gate (Case 01). After that case, at each new turning point of Korea's story, the detective arrives as a guest, and a note with a small water drop is waiting.
ending: 15 August 1945, Chongqing: the news of Japan's surrender comes. Bitna, the youngest keeper, opens the old letter box: Bun-i's first note from 1446 lies under eleven more. 'Gwangbok' means the light returns. Many people, at home and far away, known and unknown, worked and waited for this day. The letters are free again.

acts.title: THE WATER-DROP NOTES
acts.summary: 1446 to the 1860s: the King's new letters, the turtle ship before the war, the crane at Hwaseong, the rebuilt palace. In every case a note with a water drop is waiting.
acts.turningPoint: Case 04: the detective lays the notes of 1592, 1795 and 1866 side by side. The same water drop, the same way of writing: one family, not one person, writes them.

acts.title: LETTERS IN HARD TIMES
acts.summary: 1895 to 1919: the Queen's palace, the Emperor's secret letter, the reports from Harbin, the fire on the hill. Korea loses its rights, and people stand up for them.
acts.turningPoint: Case 08: Gyeongsun shows the detective the old letter box. Under the notes lies Bun-i's first note of 1446. The keepers are Bun-i's family.

acts.title: THE LIGHT RETURNS
acts.summary: The 1920s to 1945: the government in exile in Shanghai, the two watches, the poet's copies, the day of liberation. Letters are hidden, kept and read again.
acts.turningPoint: Case 11: Korean lessons have stopped in the schools, and the keeper Miri hides the box with a poet's copy. Case 12: the box is opened in Chongqing on the day the light returns.

cases.title: The Secret of the King's Letters
cases.question: Who wrote the half-burnt paper in the new letters, and what were its four groups?
cases.solution: Bun-i, a water-carrier who could not write Chinese characters, wrote the name of the King's letters on her tenth day. The groups are found as 훈, 음, 정, 민 and built by their meanings: Hunminjeongeum, the right sounds to teach the people.
cases.toNext: Bun-i's water drops: the mark every later note carries.

cases.title: The Turtle Ship Before Dawn
cases.question: Spring 1592, the navy base at Yeosu: the day before the turtle ship's cannon test, the gunpowder is gone from the store room. Who moved it, and where?
cases.solution: Made up: Seok moved the powder away from a leaking roof and left the note. History (the answer DRAGON): Yi Sun-sin's turtle ship had a plank roof like a turtle's back and a dragon head with a gun hole. His diary records the cannon test on the 12th day of the 4th lunar month of 1592; on the 13th Japanese ships reached Busan and the Imjin War began; in the 5th month his navy won the first victory at sea, at Okpo.
cases.fromPrevious: The water drop on the note is Bun-i's mark (s5_ep01_c1: the water-carrier).
cases.toNext: Seok's note is the second water-drop note.

cases.title: The Crane That Lifts Stones
cases.question: 1795, Hwaseong Fortress in Suwon: the new lifting machine is said to be broken. Is it, and who wrote the warning?
cases.solution: Made up: a foreman built the machine from the wrong drawing; Okbun left the note. History (the answer 1796): Hwaseong Fortress was begun in 1794 and finished in 1796; lifting machines like Jeong Yak-yong's geojunggi helped move the big stones, and the 1801 record book lists the workers and their pay.
cases.fromPrevious: Seok's water drop of 1592 matches this note's (s5_ep02_e1).
cases.toNext: Two notes, two hundred years apart, the same mark.

cases.title: The Palace of a Thousand Logs
cases.question: 1866, the rebuilding of Gyeongbokgung: timber marked for the palace is missing from the yard. Where did it go?
cases.solution: Made up: a dealer changed the marks on the logs; Duri left the note. History (the Daewongun's talk): the rebuilding of Gyeongbokgung began in the 4th month of 1865 under the Heungseon Daewongun and the King moved in in 1868; it cost the people dearly: money they could not refuse to give, a new coin in 1866 that pushed prices up, and farmers called to work.
cases.fromPrevious: The note is written with Sora's rule for stronger sounds (s5_ep01_e2); the water drop matches 1592 and 1795.
cases.toNext: The same drop in three centuries: a family, not one person.

cases.title: The Lights of Geoncheonggung
cases.question: Early autumn 1895, Geoncheonggung in Gyeongbokgung: the electric lamps go dark and strangers are seen in the court. What were they doing, and why is the Queen in danger?
cases.solution: Made up: strangers took the belt off the lamp machine and drew a map; Court Lady Han found it. History (the answer JAPAN): in 1895 Queen Myeongseong worked with Russia to hold back Japan's power. On 8 October 1895 men sent by Japan's minister attacked the palace and killed her (told plainly, once).
cases.fromPrevious: Duri's water-drop note of 1866 (s5_ep04_e1): the same water drop.
cases.toNext: The palace is no longer safe.

cases.title: The Emperor's Secret Letter
cases.question: Spring 1907, Gyeongun Palace: Emperor Gojong's secret letter for the peace conference in The Hague must leave the palace unseen. Where is it hidden?
cases.solution: Made up: Bongsu read the traces to the old pine's hollow. History (the answer FORCED): Emperor Gojong sent Yi Jun, Yi Sang-seol and Yi Wi-jong to the peace conference in The Hague in 1907 to tell the world that the 1905 treaty was forced on Korea. They were not let in; Yi Jun died in The Hague, and Japan forced Gojong off the throne that year.
cases.fromPrevious: Court Lady Han's water drop (s5_ep05_e1) and the strangers' map (s5_ep05_e4): the palace is watched.
cases.toNext: Korea's rights are taken; people far from Seoul keep its truth.

cases.title: Two Reports from Harbin
cases.question: Late October 1909, Harbin: two newspaper reports about An Jung-geun disagree. Which one tells the truth?
cases.solution: Made up: two newspaper reports, Mr. Pak and Mrs. Kang. History (the talk's last answer): on 26 October 1909 at Harbin Station An Jung-geun called out 'Korea, hurrah!'; in prison he began 'On Peace in East Asia', writing that he acted for Korea's independence and for peace in East Asia.
cases.fromPrevious: Bongsu's water drop (s5_ep06_e1) and the Emperor's letter (s5_ep06_e4): the 1905 treaty was forced.
cases.toNext: Ten years later, people all over Korea stand up.

cases.title: The Fire on the Hill
cases.question: March 1919, near Cheonan: Yu Gwan-sun plans a march at Aunae Market. When and how will the villages know the day?
cases.solution: Made up: the messengers, Mr. Pyo and Gyeongsun's box. History (the answer 311): Yu Gwan-sun brought the March First Movement home; a fire on Maebong hill at night was the sign, and on 1 April 1919 thousands marched for independence at Aunae Market. Her parents died that day; she was arrested and died in Seodaemun Prison in 1920 (told plainly, once).
cases.fromPrevious: Bun-i's note (s5_ep01_e3) is in the box; Mrs. Kang's note of 1909 (s5_ep07_e1).
cases.toNext: The keepers are one family. The next keeper goes to Shanghai.

cases.title: The Spy in the Shanghai Office
cases.question: 1920s, Shanghai: someone copies the Provisional Government's secret list. Who?
cases.solution: Made up: the spy Nam Giho and the copied list. History (the answer PROTECT): the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea was founded in Shanghai in April 1919; Kim Gu was its police chief from August 1919, guarding it and watching for spies, and later led it.
cases.fromPrevious: Gyeongsun's box went to Shanghai with Haesu (s5_ep08_e4).

cases.title: The Two Watches
cases.question: 29 April 1932, Shanghai: Yun Bong-gil and Kim Gu exchanged watches in the morning. Which watch is which, and what did Yun leave behind?
cases.solution: History (the answer 1932): on the morning of 29 April 1932 Yun Bong-gil gave Kim Gu his new watch and took Kim Gu's old one; that day he carried out his act at Hongkou Park (told in one plain line). Afterwards Chinese leaders, Chiang Kai-shek among them, strongly supported the Provisional Government. Yun was arrested and died in Japan in December 1932.
cases.fromPrevious: Haesu again; Kim Gu of Case 09 (s5_ep09_e4).
cases.toNext: The box goes back to Seoul with Haesu's cousin Miri.

cases.title: The Poet's Three Copies
cases.question: Late 1941, Yonhi College, Seoul: Yun Dong-ju's handwritten book of poems cannot be printed. Where is the copy he made for his friend?
cases.solution: Made up: Miri, who helps at the college, keeps the copy for one night. History (the answer KOREAN): in 1941 Yun Dong-ju copied his nineteen poems by hand in three copies, written in Korean while Korean was being pushed out of the schools; his friend Jeong Byeong-uk's copy was hidden under the floor of the family house in Gwangyang and became a book in 1948.
cases.fromPrevious: Haesu's water-drop note (s5_ep10_e1) and the letters themselves (s5_ep01): Korean is taught less and less in the schools.
cases.toNext: Miri sends the box to the family in Chongqing.

cases.title: The Day the Light Returned
cases.question: August 1945, Chongqing: the last water-drop note is in the box, but what does it say, and who is the last keeper?
cases.solution: Made up: Bitna, the trunks and the keepers' notes. History (the answer LIGHT): on 15 August 1945 Japan surrendered to the Allies; gwangbok means 'the light returns'. Kim Won-bong had worked for independence since 1919 and was the government in exile's minister of military affairs in Chongqing. No one person brought the day: the Allies' victory and many Koreans at home and abroad, most of them unknown.
cases.fromPrevious: Every water-drop note (s5_ep02_e1 to s5_ep11_e1) and Bun-i's first note.

mysteryQuestions.question: Who leaves the water-drop notes?
mysteryQuestions.answer: Bun-i's family: a keeper in every generation.

mysteryQuestions.question: Is it one person who writes them across the centuries?
mysteryQuestions.answer: No: the same mark in 1592, 1795 and 1866 cannot be one person's.

mysteryQuestions.question: What do the keepers keep?
mysteryQuestions.answer: A small wooden letter box with every note, Bun-i's first one at the bottom.

Seok's water drop of 1592 is on Okbun's note of 1795 and Duri's of 1866: a family, not one person.

The date 8.15 on Bitna's note, and the last tiles G and L.

timeline.what: King Sejong makes 28 new letters (1443); the book Hunminjeongeum is finished (1446). Case 01.
Yi Sun-sin's navy at Yeosu tests the turtle ship's cannons; the next day the Japanese army lands at Busan. Case 02.
Hwaseong Fortress is built in Suwon; Jeong Yak-yong's lifting machine helps. Case 03.
Gyeongbokgung is rebuilt under the Heungseon Daewongun. Case 04.
Queen Myeongseong is killed in an attack on the palace (the Eulmi incident). Case 05 is set weeks before.
Emperor Gojong's envoys go to The Hague; they are not let in. Case 06.
An Jung-geun's act at Harbin Station. Case 07 is set days after.
The March First Movement; Yu Gwan-sun and the Aunae Market march on 1 April. Case 08.
The Provisional Government in Shanghai; Kim Gu its police chief. Case 09.
Yun Bong-gil at Hongkou Park, Shanghai. Case 10 is set that morning.
Yun Dong-ju copies his poems by hand at Yonhi College. Case 11.

notes: The mouth words (throat, the mouth, the back of the tongue) are taught on Sora's board before they are used.
Redesigned 2026-11-07: the name read by its meanings.

Read as a player 2026-11-06: place words (under, next to, on) carry M1; Sora's board is restated in the letter, so M2 needs no outside knowledge; M3 is two number words; the final names the dragon in the Admiral's fourth line.
Hard words in the glossary (gunpowder, quartermaster, planks, spikes, navy, cannon). Dates are said as "the fourth month" (moon calendar) everywhere.

Read as a player 2026-11-06: until / after decide the timeline; the drawing is chosen by shape words (like a gate, under them, on each side), not colour; before / only after / last decide the lifting steps; the final is counting on two years and eight months from the first month of 1794.
Glossary: fortress, pulley, beam, foreman, carpenter, clerk, geojunggi.

Read as a player 2026-11-06: the lens task needs the yard board and Sora's rule, both in the letter; the count compares two lines of numbers; the timeline uses after / until / then, and the half-built palace tells the player to set aside the King moving in.
The cost is told plainly (forced gifts, high prices, hard work), never as a judgement in the Daewongun's mouth. Glossary: timber, apprentice, dealer, ruins, rebuilding, prices.
Short sentences; the key contrast is did not / did (the fire, the coal, the belt).
The knot rule is one sentence a child can apply (ten steps, one step).
The final names two countries in one sentence (works with Russia / holds back Japan): the hardest line of the case, helped by the feedback and the glossary (power, minister).
The Queen's death is one plain line in the ending, without detail.
Place words (not to the steps, on rough bark, by a root) carry the trace puzzle.
First/After/Then/Last and one Do not line carry the route.
The lock word forced is taught in the intro and the lid (Japan made Korea sign it; Korea did not choose it); envoy, treaty and conference are in the glossary.
Two short records of four lines each; one line differs.
Before/after words carry the timeline; the noon train is the key.
The act is named once in the intro, plainly, and never described.
independence and peace in East Asia appear only in the ending, with the glossary.
The messengers' answers are 4 to 9 words; the three questions are short and repeated.
Gwan-sun's plan teaches the night before / in the morning / when; the final asks one step of reasoning (March has thirty-one days) and says it in the letter.
independence, messenger, elders and dusk are in the glossary; the history lines in the ending are one plain sentence each.
The candle sum (half of four hours from eleven) is the hardest step; the second hint says how to think without the answer.
Clock words (half past, a quarter past) are taught by the sign-out book and checked against Mission 1.
provisional, exile, spy and clerk are in the glossary; Kim Gu's lines are under 12 words.
Order words (first, after, before that, at the end) are the whole of Mission 1.
Picture choices are told apart by words (scratches, smooth, strap), not colour.
Years in words (nineteen nineteen, nineteen thirty-two) are the final's reading; the act at Hongkou Park is one plain line, without detail.
Lines are short; the hard words (spine, subject, dictionary, list) are in the glossary.
M2 compares two short records line by line: three lines agree word for word, one is not true, and the card's last words turn it into black and white keys.
M3 reads its numbers on Yun's list (copy 2 of 3, 18 + 1 opening poem): a small sum, with 2 of 3 its own trap.
The final answer KOREAN follows from the copy's pages (the King's letters) and Case 01's reason for the letters; wrong words get their own feedback.
M1 asks for two features together (ONE strap and a round brass lock); each wrong trunk has one of them.
M2 uses before/after/oldest/on top only; no years to compare beyond the two fixed notes.
M3 teaches month names as numbers (August is month eight) and the Korean date order.
The ending says liberation plainly in short lines: Japan surrendered to the Allies; many Koreans worked for it; gwangbok means the light returns.
Written by Claude Code for PART 10 (2026-11-06): Season 5 whole, Case 01 kept as it is, Cases 02-12 made with the season factory.

Real people, years, places and events follow the dossier's checked facts; the detective's cases, the keepers, the letter box and the water-drop notes are made up. The player never changes what happened.
Ages 8-12: no violence is shown; deaths in history are told in one plain line in a reveal, never described. Liberation in 1945 is never one person's work.

Policy (user, 2026-11-06): every case ends in a verifiable historical fact. The mystery starts from the real event, the clues teach its background, the final mission's answer is the key fact (the person's real achievement, action or meaning), and the ending, case summary and REAL HISTORY state it. The made-up mystery is solved; the real outcome never changes. Made-up lines and clues are never shown as records.
